The surah opens with a critical attack on those who cheat in weights and measures: woe and destruction are upon those who give short measure (al-mutaffifin). Here the destruction is stated as a decision, that their ruin has already been decreed, or it is a curse upon them; the meaning of both is one and the same, because a curse from Allah is also a decision.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 83, verses 2–3:

The next two verses define the mutaffifin (those who give short measure and weight), that is, who the one who cheats in measure and weight is.

Alladhina idha ........................ yakhsiroon (83:2-3): "These are the people who, when they take from people, take in full, but when they measure or weigh out for them, they give less." When they are buyers, they take in full with great cunning; and when they are sellers, they give less.

It is surprising, and of particular significance, that in this Meccan surah, with such emphasis, the issue of short measure and weight is discussed, because in the Meccan surahs the discussion is generally about universal and fundamental beliefs and principles: the proof of Tawhid (Oneness of God), the unrestricted will of Allah, Allah's control over all creation and the entire universe, the reality of revelation and the office of prophethood, the reality of the Hereafter and reckoning, and, in general, the cultivation of moral sentiments, especially those sentiments that are closely connected with these fundamental beliefs and principles. As for discussing a particular moral issue in detail, such as the issue of giving short measure and short weight, and other irregularities in dealings, this is not found in the Meccan surahs. All these matters came in the Madinan surahs, when the Islamic system of government had been established and had begun to address economic, social and societal problems, because this was the general approach of the Islamic method.

Therefore, it is necessary to explain why the Quran took up this issue, departing from this general rule. The truth is that from these few short verses it appears that there were certain reasons for this.

From these verses one thing becomes clear: when Islam came, a cruel system of short measure and weight was present in Makkah in a frightful form. The elders (kubara) of Makkah practised this. Their control extended over the trade of the whole of Arabia, indeed of East and West. These elders were owners of vast enterprises. They had even spread a network of hoarding. These people directed their journeys in summer and winter towards Syria and the coast of Yemen, and at various occasions they had also organised trade fairs. For example, at the time of Hajj, the market of Ukaz was held, in which, alongside extensive commercial activity, literary and historical activities also flourished; people also recited boasts and poetry.

The verses show that Allah here issues a severe warning to these elder criminals that destruction is over your heads. Likewise, a declaration of war is made against them, which shows that those who committed this evil were people of the higher classes, and they had such a social standing that they would compel people to give them less. The Quran used the expression (yaktaloona 'ala al-nas), in which the word "ala" carries the sense of superiority, meaning that by virtue of their high position they imposed short measure upon people, and when they took from them, they took more by force. If they had taken in full, this would not have been objectionable and would not have been mentioned. That is, whatever they wished, they took by force. And when they gave to people, because of their political and social position they gave less, because those people were not in a position to obtain their rights in full, since these elders held political and tribal superiority, and due to their economic superiority people were compelled to accept their oppression. They engaged in hoarding and then sold to people at high prices and gave them out, as is a feature of today's commercial system. In short, a clear oppressive system of tatfif was operating in Makkah, and so it was challenged.

In this Meccan society, during the very earliest days of the call of Islam, the attention paid to this issue shows what the temperament of the religion of Islam is. It also shows that this religion is a complete system of life that dominates every sphere of life, whether theoretical or practical. And the foundation of this system rests upon profound moral principles that are placed very deep within this system. That is why Islam, even in those early days, disapproved of this wrong practice, because in mutual dealings it was open immorality. Although in that period Islam did not have collective leadership and authority, there was no government, and the Islamic Shari'ah was not in force, yet Islam, in perfect accord with its temperament, raised this voice against this evil. And it declared that for those who cheat in measure and weight there is destruction and ruin. Those who did this work were the chiefs of Makkah, those in power and authority. They had spiritual sovereignty over the people, they were the guardians of the creed of shirk, and they also held economic superiority in Makkah. Despite the leadership and sovereignty of these people, Islam raised its voice against their oppression and fraud. And it raised its voice in favour of the poor masses who were being exploited, and this exploitation they were carrying out on the basis of the religious ideas they had instilled in the minds of these masses. The voice that Islam raised was the natural voice of Islam, in perfect accord with the temperament of the Islamic system, and it was a voice that was awakening the sleeping masses. The Islamic movement raised this voice at a time when its followers were oppressed and confined in Makkah, while those against whom it was raised were dominant over society and held economic, religious and financial superiority.

From this we get a very realistic reason for why the polytheists of Makkah stood as an insurmountable obstacle in the face of Islam and the call of Islam. There is no doubt that they knew that this new doctrine that Muhammad (ﷺ) was presenting was not merely a creed and verbal affirmation that Allah is One and Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Messenger of Allah, and that, abandoning idols and images, one should worship and serve only one God. It was not so; rather, they knew that this creed and doctrine was uprooting all the foundations of jahiliyyah, and that along with it all their interests were being destroyed, and that their honour, status and authority were under serious threat from this creed. The temperament of this system does not accept duality. Nor does this system merge with secular elements whose connection is not with heavenly guidance and concepts, and this system eliminates all the earthly material upon which the system of jahiliyyah is established. That is why the people of Makkah began a war on all fronts against this new system, and this struggle did not stop either in the period before the Hijrah or in later times; it never ended. This struggle was in fact a war of culture. These people were fighting against Islamic culture. It was not merely a religious, ideological war.

Those who are blocking the path of the authority of the Islamic system have understood this reality well in every age and every place. They have understood well the consequences of the dominance of the Islamic system, and that is precisely why they have tried to prevent the Islamic system from dominating. These people knew, and know, that their false ways, their oppressive interests, their lost self-serving power and their deviation, in short all these things, are destined to end upon the dominance of the Islamic system, because it is a straightforward and extremely noble system.

In comparison with other people, these rebels, transgressors and cheats, whatever form this cheating and oppression takes, whether financial oppression or oppression in other rights and duties, these rebels and transgressors fear the Islamic system more than others, because it is an extremely just and pure system. This system accepts no bargaining and no compromise on human rights, nor does it decide on a "fifty-fifty" or "give and take" basis.

Those who pledged allegiance at the Second Pledge of Aqabah before the Hijrah had understood this very reality well. Ibn Ishaq says: "And 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn Qatadah told me that when the people gathered to pledge allegiance at the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), 'Abbas ibn 'Ubadah ibn Nadlah al-Ansari, a member of Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, said: 'O people of Khazraj, do you know upon what you are pledging allegiance to this man?' They said: 'Yes, we know.' He said: 'The reality is that you and we are going to fight the red and the black. If your opinion is that when we suffer financial penalty and our nobles are killed, you will abandon him, then leave him now; if you abandon him later, you will be ruined in this world and the Hereafter. But if you are determined that losing wealth and the killing of nobles is acceptable to us, then pledge allegiance. By Allah, this is better than the world and the Hereafter.' The pledgers said: 'We accept it even with the loss of wealth and the killing of nobles.' Upon this he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what reward will we get if we fulfil this covenant?' He (ﷺ) said: 'Paradise.' They said: 'Extend your hand.' He (ﷺ) extended his hand and took the pledge of the people."

In short, those who made the pledge of 'Aqabah also understood the temperament of this religion, and the elders of Quraysh also understood that this religion, like the edge of a sword, stands firmly upon the principles of justice and fairness. It does not tolerate oppression and rebellion in any way, it tolerates neither transgression of limits and rebellion, nor arrogance and pride, and it does not tolerate oppression, injustice, deceit and exploitation in the name of religion. Therefore, every person who is rebellious, a transgressor, arrogant, or an exploiter is an enemy of this religion, of its call, and of its callers.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 83, verses 4–6:

"Do these people not think that they will be raised again on a mighty day, the day when all mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds?" (83:4–6)

The case of these people is very strange. The mere belief that we shall one day stand before the Lord of the worlds, and that on that day none will have authority except the Lord of the worlds, none will be a master besides Him, the whole matter will await the decision of Allah alone, and there will be no protector or helper except Allah, was by itself sufficient to keep them from this vile act of cheating in measure, from consuming the wealth of people by falsehood, from making their power a means of oppression, and from usurping the rights of others. Yet they continue to practise cheating, as though they have no belief at all that they must present themselves before Allah. This is a strange way of behaving.

In the first paragraph of this surah these people were called al-Mutaffifin, meaning those who cheat in measure, and in the second paragraph they were called al-Fujjar, meaning the wicked. Here they are placed among the ranks of the wicked, and it is explained what their days and nights are like, what their standing is with Allah, how they are in this life, how they will be in the Hereafter, and what kinds of conditions await them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 83, verses 7–9:

Those people do not believe that they will be raised on the great Day of Resurrection. For this reason the Qur'an, in a manner of stern rebuke and reproach, prevents them from this, and with great emphasis tells them that their deeds are being recorded in a book. And to make this point even more emphatic, it also tells where this book is kept, and it is also stated that when the book of these wicked and sinful people is presented before them on that great day, a great destruction will befall them.

﴿Nay, indeed! The record of the wicked is surely in Sijjin. And what will make you know what Sijjin is? It is a book inscribed. Woe on that day to the deniers.﴾ (83:7–10). Fujjar (wicked, sinful people) are those who transgress all limits in sin and wrongdoing; the meaning is hidden within the very sound of the word fujjar itself. Their "book" refers to their record of deeds. Human beings do not have knowledge of its nature and condition. It is among the unseen matters, and about it we can only say what the one who is truthful in reporting (the Prophet ﷺ) has informed us. The Qur'an has stated that there is a record of the deeds of the wicked and that it is in Sijjin. It is the Qur'anic style to pose a question in order to make a matter frightening.

﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ (83:8). The purpose is to convey the impression that this matter is beyond the limits of your comprehension and far from it, very great, and greater than the scope of your understanding. However, the Qur'an nonetheless clarifies that

﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ (83:7): the record of the sinful is in Sijjin, which is a specific place, although its exact nature is not known to human beings. Thus the readers are given a certain assurance that this record has been prepared and exists, and this is what is intended here.

﴿It is a book inscribed﴾ (83:9): the detail of the record is that the record of the wicked has been prepared, and nothing can be added to or subtracted from it. Only on that great day will it be opened. So take heed.

"Woe on that Day to the deniers" (83:10). "On that Day, woe to those who deny." And the deniers are also described.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 83, verses 11–13:

﴿Alladhina...﴾ to ﴿al-awwalin﴾ (83:11–13): ﴿And none deny it except every transgressor, sinful.﴾ ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "These are tales of the ancients."﴾

They level this accusation because the Qur'an brings the stories and circumstances of earlier nations as lessons. Through them it points out the Divine Way (sunnah Ilahiyyah) operating in this universe, and this Way seizes people like an unalterable law.

After this insolence and denial, a rebuke and warning now comes. It begins with ﴿Kalla﴾ ("No indeed!"), and in it the real cause and reason for their conduct is stated: why they commit injustice and deny the truth. The answer is that they have become heedless, and their hearts have become distorted and rusted over.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 83, verse 14:

Kalla bal ........................ yaksibun (83:14) "Never! Rather, upon their hearts is the rust of what they have been earning (by their evil deeds)." That is, the sins and disobediences they commit have covered their hearts.

When a person commits sin, his heart gradually becomes rusted and darkened. In this way a thick veil falls over it, the heart is hidden from light, and its perception gradually diminishes, until perception itself is lost.

Imam al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan, from Qan'aq, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When a servant commits a sin, a black spot is placed on his heart. If he repents, it is cleansed; and if he returns to sin, the blackness increases." Imam al-Tirmidhi called it hasan sahih. And the words of Imam al-Nasa'i are: "When a person commits a mistake, a black spot falls upon his heart. If he withdraws from the evil, seeks forgiveness and repents, his heart is polished. If he repeats that evil, the spot increases, until this blackness overspreads his whole heart. This is the rust of which Allah, the Exalted, speaks."

Kalla bal ........................ yaksibun (83:14)? Never! Rather, upon their hearts is the rust of their evil deeds.

Hasan al-Basri said: "This is sin upon sin, until the heart becomes blind and then dies."

This is the state of those who deny, and this is the cause of their denial and their wickedness. Now the mention of their fate on that tremendous day follows. Their outcome on that tremendous day, which is taking place, is in keeping with their wickedness and their denial.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 83, verses 15–17:

"Nay! Indeed, on that Day they will be veiled from their Lord. Then they will surely enter the Fire. Then it will be said to them: This is what you used to deny."

Immorality, sin and transgression had covered their hearts. In the world, their hearts had become distant from the awareness of the Lord, the Exalted, and sins had made their lives dim and dark; they conducted themselves in life as if they were blind. Now, in the Hereafter, their end is also natural and fitting to their state. In the Hereafter they have been deprived of the great blessing of beholding their Lord. This will be a great deprivation. In the Resurrection, this blessing will be granted only to the person whose soul has become pure and clear, and because of this purity, all veils between him and his Lord will be removed. It is about these very people that Surah al-Qiyamah says:

"Faces that Day will be radiant, looking towards their Lord." The veil from their Lord in the Resurrection will be a punishment greater than the punishment of the Resurrection itself. It will be the greatest of all deprivations, and it will be the worst end for a human being's humanity that his humanity remains deprived of joining and reaching his Generous Lord. For when anyone is deprived of reaching the Generous Lord, he loses his distinctly human qualities and falls to such a degree that he becomes deserving and worthy of Hell.

"Then they will surely enter the Blazing Fire" (16). But along with this entry into Hell, there will also be their reproach, and this will be even more bitter than the punishment.

"Then it will be said to them: This is what you used to deny" (17).

Now, the opposite page is presented after this. It is the consistent manner of the Qur'an to generally present both faces of the picture of good and evil, so that through the contrast of beauty and ugliness people may understand the matter well, the truth may become fixed in their minds, and the end of both the good and the wicked may be brought before them.

"Nay!" (kallā) here is a particle of rebuke and reproach, and it refers back to what precedes it.

Then it will be said: "This is what you used to deny." (83:17) As a conclusion to this, it is said: "Nay! It cannot be so." And after this, the discussion of the righteous begins, and it comes in a positive and emphatic manner.

Just as it was said earlier that the record of the wicked is in Sijjin, so here it is said that the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin. The abrār (the righteous, the virtuous) are those who are obedient and who perform every good deed. They are brought forward here in contrast to the disobedient and the transgressors.

From the word ʿIlliyyin, the concept of loftiness and elevation comes to mind, and from this we can infer that Sijjin carries the sense of decline, lowness and degradation. Then comes a frightening question, which shows that the one addressed does not know what ʿIlliyyin is. The meaning is that you cannot even conceive of those heights; that station is beyond the limits of your comprehension.

Leaving this suggestive atmosphere, the discourse now turns to the record of the righteous. What it is, is as follows.

Here, Sayyid Qutb says: "A written book which is watched over by the closest angels." The meaning of "written" (marqum) has already been explained earlier. Here there is only this additional point: the closest angels oversee this book. This gives the impression that this book is extremely pure, extremely worthy of honour, and of very high rank, a book in which the closest angels of Allah are constantly present. And since this book contains a mention of the very highest morals and deeds, it is a source of life's delight for those closest angels, and they will write accordingly. The mention of this atmosphere of the book is made so that it is understood to be a worthy book.

After the mention of this worthy book, the text now speaks of the righteous (al-abrar) themselves, who are the possessors of this good record of deeds, and mentions the blessings and honours among which they will dwell.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 83, verse 22:

"Indeed the righteous will be in bliss" (83:22). This bliss (naʿīm) stands in contrast to the blazing fire (jaḥīm).

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 83, verse 23:

"On couches, looking on" (83:23). That is, they will be in a most honoured station. And in that station they will roam wherever they wish. Their gaze will not be fearful because of humiliation and disgrace, nor will they close their eyes out of exhaustion. These people will be seated on couches and cushions, gazing, just as people sit in the bridal chamber. Among the Arabs, this was regarded as the highest level of luxury, blessing and comfort: to be in a bridal chamber, seated at ease on high cushions, because the life of an Arab was generally one of hard toil. This is merely an image of worldly life. What will be in the Hereafter is beyond imagination in its elevation and loftiness. It will be higher than the highest of their conceptions, and higher than the highest notions and experiences of the earth and of this world.

Amid these blessings they will also be physically tender and delicate, and the effects of this delicacy, ease, joy and prosperity will appear upon their faces. Every person will be witnessing this.

﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾ .................... (24:83)

"You will notice in their faces the freshness of delight." (24:83)

The following is the English translation of the Urdu passage:

"They will be given to drink of a pure wine, sealed (25) [the verse says 'sealed'], whose seal is musk" (83:25).

Rahiq means pure and clear wine, free from any admixture and without any turbidity. The description of this wine as sealed, with its seal made of musk, shows that it will be in containers, and these containers will be sealed and stamped, and will be opened at the time of drinking. From this it is understood that it will be prepared with great care and purity, and sealing it with musk indicates that it will be clear and pleasant in taste. These are the attributes described in terms with which man is familiar in this world, but when the people of faith enter Paradise, their taste will be free from the taste of this world, because the taste of this world is extremely limited.

Wa mizājuhu ... al-muqarrabūn (83:28): "And its admixture will be of Tasnīm, a spring from which those brought near (to Allah) will drink." Before this conclusion, in the midst of it, an important guidance is given, and that guidance is:

Wa fī dhālika ... al-mutanāfisūn (83:26): "And for this let those who desire to outdo others strive to outdo one another." This is a profound allusion, and within it lies a whole world of meaning.

These are the cheats, who devour the wealth of people by false means, who have no concern for the Hereafter, and who deny the reckoning of the Day of Judgement; and because of their immorality, their sins and their injustice, blackness has covered their hearts. These people compete with one another for the goods and chattels of this world; each one of them wants to surpass the others in the goods and chattels of this world, and wants to gather the world as much as possible. Therefore he oppresses and is caught up in wickedness and debauchery. And he dies for this perishable paraphernalia, although the truth is that the wealth and property of this world is not worthy at all of being contested over. If someone does wish to compete and outdo others, he should strive to outdo others in the paraphernalia of the Last Day and the Hereafter.

Wa fī dhālika ... al-mutanāfisūn (83:26): "Those who wish to outdo others should outdo one another in acquiring that which pertains to the Hereafter." Because this is precisely what the believer seeks. This is the goal towards which they should race, and this is the target in which they should surpass all others.

The equipment of this world, however great and however lofty its rank may be, is insignificant and worthless in comparison with the equipment of the Hereafter. This entire world holds not even the value of a mosquito's wing in the sight of Allah. The Hereafter is weighty in the measures of Allah. Therefore the Hereafter alone is the true and valued reality for whose attainment it is fitting to outdo one another, and not this world.

It is a strange thing that the spirits of those who compete for the Hereafter become very elevated, whereas those who compete for this world fall down because of envy and enmity among themselves. Their spirit falls, and because of the striving and competition of those who strive for the Hereafter, this whole world also becomes filled with goodness and blessing, and it becomes a pure abode for all. Whereas if competition is for worldly aims, then hatred and enmity arise. People tear one another apart in the way that creeping things devour one another, and the life of righteous people in such an environment becomes extremely difficult. From every side their legs are pulled, and from every side they are torn.

It is not a correct notion that if we compete and vie with one another only for the Hereafter, this world will become ruined and destroyed, as some worldly-minded people think. The Islamic conception is that this world is a field for the Hereafter. Here the sowing of the crop takes place, and in the Hereafter the harvest is reaped. To populate and develop this world with reform and piety, in accordance with the Islamic system of life, is, according to the Islamic doctrine of vicegerency on earth (khilāfat-i-arḍī), the aim and objective of a believer. Islam believes in the progress of the Hereafter through the progress of this world. This is the Islamic doctrine of worship: that in the whole life of this world, obeying Allah is the very purpose of human creation.

Wa mā khalaqtu ... li-ya'budūn (Adh-Dhāriyāt 51:56): "And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me." (For details see Surah Adh-Dhāriyāt, Para 27.)

Wa fī dhālika ... al-mutanāfisūn (83:26): "Those who wish to outdo one another should outdo one another in that." This is a guidance which raises the gaze of the people of this world from this lowly and worthless earth and fixes it upon the Hereafter. While in practice, they, while discharging the office of human vicegerency in this very world, are also occupied in the building and development of this earth. Its example is that Muslims are occupied in purifying the filth found in this world, and also keep their skirts clear of that filth.

The truth is that human life in this world is very brief, whereas in the world of the Hereafter human life is long, and knowledge of its end belongs to Allah alone. Then the equipment of this world is also limited, whereas the equipment of Paradise is so abundant and unlimited that it is beyond human comprehension. The level of equipment and comfort in this world is also known and limited, whereas the comfort of the Hereafter is unlimited. The arena of the Hereafter is very vast and the arena of this world very limited. There is also a very great difference between the aims of the two. The profit and loss of the two are also very different. Therefore the competition is also different. And the command is: Wa fī dhālika fal-yatanāfasi al-mutanāfisūn (83:26): "And for this let those who desire to outdo others strive to outdo one another." Here the descriptions of the rewards of the righteous and the virtuous in the Hereafter became somewhat lengthy, and these were explained because in the society of Makkah they were the victims of oppression and cruelty at the hands of the wicked and the transgressors. They were being harmed, they were being mocked, and injustices were being done to them; therefore the details of the rewards prepared for them were also given. And in return for mockery, the disbelievers too will be mocked; at that time they will see that the righteous have received those rewards in full.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 83, verse 29:

The scenes of the criminals mocking the believers, their hostile acts and transgressions against them, which the Qur'an has perhaps recorded here, especially their remark that the Muslims are misguided people, are all practical scenes of Makkan society. But it is also a reality that the workers of every movement for the establishment of the religion (iqamat-i-deen) face these same circumstances and such derisive remarks. In every age and every generation this has been the situation. When we look today at the conditions of our own age, it appears that these verses may have been revealed just now, fitting our present circumstances. This shows that the temperament of the wicked and the immoral is alike, and their stance against the people of truth is always the same. The difference of time and place makes no difference in this.

﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ (29:83). "They used to" — this "used to" has enveloped centuries within its wrap. Now this is a matter being spoken of in the Hereafter. They are seeing with their own eyes the blessings of the people of Paradise. Here, in the Hereafter, they are being reminded: you used to adopt this attitude. Do you remember?

They used to laugh at the believers in mockery, saying: these are the believers, these are the "righteous" (salih), these are the "righteous ones" (salihin). Why did they laugh? Either because these people were poor and destitute, spoke of revolution, and wore rags. Or because they were being struck from every side, were in prisons, and could not even defend themselves. Or because these people did not take part in their follies, and to those people all these things seemed ridiculous. Thus they rained arrows of taunts and derision upon the believers. They would cause them distress, persecute them, subject them to violence, and mock them in the most base and vulgar manner. The believers were deeply affected by this and felt pain, but they would be patient. They adopted lofty moral conduct and would deflect matters with the utmost decency.

When they passed by them, they would wink at one another (as a gesture of mockery).

That is, they would signal with their eyes, or with their hands, or make some movement that was known among them as a way of ridiculing others. Such a base act would express their disrespect and impudence; it was a gesture outside the bounds of decency. The purpose of such gestures was to break the hearts of the Muslims, to shame them, and to make them despair of the success of this movement. For this reason these people would make such signs and frivolous movements.

"And when they returned to their families, they returned jesting (fakihin)." That is, after inflicting torment on the believers and mocking them, when they tired of it they would return to their homes "fakihin" (31) — that is, returning with relish. They took delight in these actions, returning with great pleasure and swaggering, and they were intensely gratified by their own base deeds and mischief. Yet had their conscience been alive, it would have reproached them, and they would have felt remorse for these acts. They had no awareness at all of how contemptible an act they were committing and how vile their conduct was. This is the ultimate extent of the distortion of heart and vision and the death of conscience.

"And when they saw them, they would say, 'Indeed, these are misguided,'" (83:32).

And it is most astonishing that these people have now begun to speak on the subject of guidance and misguidance, and, in their own estimation, they call the people of truth and guidance the people of error and misguidance, and they pass this judgment with absolute certainty and in a contemptuous manner.

"Indeed, these are surely misguided" (83:32).

It is the nature of immorality and depravity that it does not stop at any limit; it is not ashamed of any statement, and it is not embarrassed by any deed. When such sinners and wrongdoers accuse the believers, who are the standard of righteousness, of being misguided, this shows that sinners and wrongdoers do not stop at any limit and are shameless.

The Noble Qur'an neither engages the believers in debate nor in disputation. It does not refute this slander, because it is such a base and vile statement that it does not require serious attention. However, the Noble Qur'an does certainly make a serious mockery of those people who poke their noses into a matter with which they have no connection. What have they to do with guidance and misguidance? And who appointed them to watch over the Muslims?

﴿Although they had not been sent as guardians over them﴾ (33:83). Neither were the affairs of the Muslims entrusted to them, nor were they their supervisors, nor were they questioned about the circumstances and conditions of the believers. Therefore, this remark of theirs about the Muslims is a senseless statement.

The scene of how the criminals used to treat the believers in the world ends here with this serious mockery, and now the scene of the Day of Judgment is presented before us: behold how the believers are enjoying themselves in Paradise.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 83, verses 34–35:

﴿So today those who believe laugh at the disbelievers, [as they sit] on couches, looking on.﴾ (83:34–35) What kind of day is today, when the disbelievers are deprived of, and veiled from, a blessing such as the vision of the Lord? They grieve greatly over this deprivation, and because of it their humanity has collapsed and they have become fit for Hell. And upon this descent into Hell, they will also be humiliated and rebuked.

﴿Is this not the reward that you used to deny?﴾ (83:36) Today is such that the people of faith sit upon raised couches, watching the condition of the disbelievers, and they enjoy everlasting blessings. They are served with sealed, pure and clear wine, and the seal of that sealed wine will be of musk, and it will be mixed with the pleasant water of the spring of Tasnim. Today, seeing the condition of the disbelievers, the people of faith will smile.

They grieve greatly over this deprivation, and because of it their humanity has collapsed and they have become fit for Hell. And upon this descent into Hell, they will also be humiliated and rebuked.

﴿Is this not the reward that you used to deny?﴾ (83:36) Today is such that the people of faith sit upon raised couches, watching the condition of the disbelievers, and they enjoy everlasting blessings. They are served with sealed, pure and clear wine, and the seal of that sealed wine will be of musk, and it will be mixed with the pleasant water of the spring of Tasnim. Today, seeing the condition of the disbelievers, the people of faith will smile.

Once again the Quran engages in a serious kind of humour.

"Has the reward of the disbelievers been paid in full for what they used to do?" (83:36). Yes, has the reward been given to them for the deeds they used to do? Did they receive their reward for what they had been doing? They did not receive any reward at all. The meaning of the word "thawab" (reward) is a good recompense, and we have just left them in Hell, where they have received the punishment for their deeds. So this punishment is, as it were, their "thawab". By using the word "thawab", the Quran has made a mockery of them in a way whose sting they feel in the depths of their hearts.

Now let us pause a little before this scene, whose images are full of movement. This is the scene of those people who in this world committed crimes against the Muslims and the Islamic movement. Earlier, in describing the reward of the righteous (abrar), the Quran had dwelt at some length, and had dwelt at length on the scenes of their comfort and luxury. This extended description and detail had, in its effect, excellent qualities, and psychologically and intellectually it was the best consolation for the Muslims working in the difficult conditions of Makkah. In Makkah this handful of Muslims were facing severe hardships. They were being tormented, and all kinds of oppression were being inflicted upon them, and these things certainly had a deep effect on them. They needed to be reassured, to have their spirits raised, and to be helped.

The details of the persecution that the polytheists were inflicting upon the Muslims were important for the Muslims. They were a kind of consolation: that their Lord was surely watching, and that He would not leave these afflictions as they were. Although the disbelievers were being given respite for the time being, the thought that Allah is watching was sufficient to console the hearts of the believers. Through it, the hearts of the believers were soothed, knowing that Allah sees how those who mock the believers are mocking them, how the people of Makkah are inflicting every kind of torment upon them, and how they are taking pleasure in their pains and sufferings. How these base people display their vileness, and feel no shame at all; yet the Lord of the believers sees all of this and is recording it in the Quran for ever and ever. This is because such a state of affairs deserves, in the sight of Allah, to be recorded for ever. The truth is that when this feeling arose in the hearts of the believers, all their grief and suffering was relieved, and all sorrow and anguish came to an end.

Then their Lord makes a serious jest of these criminals. These audacious criminals may not perceive this humour, because their nature has been distorted and their hearts have become rusted, indeed blackened, by their evil deeds. But the sensitive hearts of the believers, and hearts trembling with the fear of Allah, give importance to this humour and value it; it is a soothing remedy for their pains and sorrows, and it brings them joy.

These believers also take note of the fact that they have a station with their Lord. They also see that there are blessings for them in the Gardens, and that in the higher realm, in the presence of the Divine court, they have an exalted rank and honour. Then they also see what the condition of their enemies is in the Hereafter, and that they are abased and disgraced before Allah, worthless, and what humiliating punishment awaits them in those scenes of the Resurrection. They see these scenes, and from them they gain the certainty of what their own condition will be on the Day of Resurrection. At that time the Muslims were few, they were being persecuted, they were weak, they were being mocked, and because of their small number and weakness they were enduring every kind of affliction. Therefore, through the impressions of these scenes and the certainty gained from them, all these bitternesses would diminish, and their sorrow and pain would lessen. Because of these circumstances, scenes, and the certainty that resulted from them, some believers even found sweetness amid those bitternesses, and felt that they were actually seeing in this very world what is mentioned in these verses.

However, from the biography of the Companions (sahaba) (ra) it is known that the more they suffered, the more the criminals oppressed them and mocked them in base ways, all these hardships they were bearing for one single goal: that they would receive Paradise, and their opposing disbelievers would receive Hell; and the conditions of these two groups in this world would be completely reversed in the Hereafter. This is the very thing that the Prophet (ﷺ) had promised to the believers who had pledged allegiance at his hand, and for the path in which they were sacrificing their wealth and their lives.

As for the matter that you will also be granted dominance in this world, and that you will conquer lands, the mention of this in the Quran during the Makkan period is very rare. That is, its purpose is to console the believers and to raise their spirits.

The real point is that in Makkah the Quran was preparing individuals who would be able to bear the responsibilities of this trust and this ideology, and these individuals were to be so strong, so capable, so sincere and so full of character that they would sacrifice all the worldly interests for this path. Their sole aim would be success in the Hereafter, and they would seek only the pleasure of Allah. They would be people ready to spend their entire life in this world in hardship and difficulty, ready to bear oppression and cruelty, ready to offer every kind of sacrifice, and in this world they would seek no reward, not even seeking an Islamic revolution or the dominance of Islam in this world, and there would not even be in their hearts a desire to come to power. The Quran had in view the preparation of such a sincere community.

And when such a community came into being, for which there was no aim among the purposes of this brief worldly journey, except that something might come without their desire, and whose goal was solely the attainment of the reward of the Hereafter, and whose belief was that the final decision between truth and falsehood would be made in the Hereafter, when such a community came into being, and Allah knew that this community was truthful and its intention was pure, and that it had made true the purpose for which it had given its allegiance, then in this world too the help of Allah came for its support. And this help came so that it might fulfil the trust of the Islamic call and the right of the Islamic system of life. No worldly interest had been promised to such a community, and there was no worldly desire in the heart of this community that it should be given this or that. This community had become so sincere that its sole aim was the pleasure of Allah. The verses that mention success on this earth are all Madani verses, and the Madani circumstances arose at a time when the believers had no desire for such circumstances, nor were they waiting for them. This help came when the will of Allah required that the Islamic system of life be established in practical form upon the earth, so that the people of that time and of coming times might practically see Islam. This help was not a reward for the trials, hardships, afflictions and sacrifices of the believers. It was simply a decision of Allah, and we are now trying to understand its wisdom. (1)
